conversation.content:
Good morning, I’m Susan, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use the Edinburgh Postpartum Depression Scale (EPDS)—a short, 10-item questionnaire that looks at mood, anxiety, and self-harm thoughts during the past week. It’s completely confidential; anything you share helps us decide what support or resources might help you feel more like yourself again. I’ll read each question once, and you can answer in your own words—no right or wrong replies. Ready to start?

In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? I still laugh sometimes—like when my baby makes those little milk-drunk faces—but it feels a little forced. I’d say I’ve managed to laugh a couple of times this week, but it’s not the easy, light feeling I used to have.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Well… like I said, I can still chuckle when the baby does something cute, but it doesn’t feel as natural or lift my mood the way it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Most days I don’t really feel that spark. I’ll plan little things—like taking the baby for a walk—but once the time comes it just feels like another chore. I guess I’m going through the motions more than actually looking forward to anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah, I catch myself doing that. Like, if the baby’s fussy and won’t settle, I’ll think maybe I missed his sleepy cues or didn’t feed him right—little stuff that probably isn’t my fault, but I still feel guilty. It’s not constant, maybe a few times this week, but it sticks with me.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… my mind keeps jumping to scary “what-ifs” about the baby—like what if he stops breathing or isn’t gaining enough weight—even when everything looks fine at the check-ups. I’ll be sitting there feeding him and suddenly feel my heart racing for no clear reason. It’s happened several nights this week.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times—mostly in the evenings—this wave of panic just hits. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly feel like I can’t catch my breath, like something awful is about to happen even though nothing’s wrong. It passes, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah, that sums it up. Some days it feels like as soon as I finish one feeding, the next is already due, laundry’s piled up, and I haven’t eaten a real meal. I manage, but it’s like I’m barely treading water—by bedtime I’m drained and wondering how I’ll do it all again tomorrow.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m that unhappy, but I do have trouble sleeping. I’ll lie there listening to every squeak the baby makes, or replay little worries in my head, and it takes me a long time to drift off—then I jolt awake at the slightest noise. It’s happened maybe four nights this week.
I have felt sad or miserable

I get spells of feeling down—usually when I’m alone with the baby and the house is quiet. It’s not all day, but a few times this week I’ve caught myself tearing up for no real reason and thinking, “Is this supposed to be easier by now?”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I haven’t cried a lot—just once, maybe twice. One night the baby wouldn’t settle, my partner was asleep, and I felt this sudden wave of “I can’t do this.” The tears came for a minute, but I wiped them off and kept rocking him.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’m tired and overwhelmed sometimes, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself—I just want to feel more like me again.

You've shared that motherhood hasn't felt as joyful as you expected-laughter comes less easily, activities you plan feel like chores, and waves of worry or even panic arrive without warning. You're working hard to care for your baby, but you often feel overwhelmed, find yourself tearing up at quiet moments, and lie awake running through "what-ifs" even when you're exhausted. It's clear you love your baby and are doing your best, yet the emotional weight is heavy right now.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to laugh; humor feels forced and no longer elevates mood, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports no enjoyment or anticipation, describing activities as chores and "hardly at all" looking forward to things.</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame several times this week, matching 'Yes, some of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive worries about the baby and physical anxiety (heart racing) occurring "several nights this week," matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes unmistakable panic episodes occurring repeatedly, matching the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed by daily tasks, barely managing, and being drained—aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Response describes frequent, noticeable episodes of sadness occurring multiple times in the week, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 18 places you well above the ≥14 cutoff indicating probable major depression; endorsed items map to five <sym>depressive symptoms</sym> (low mood, loss of interest, guilt, tearfulness, trouble coping) and two <sym>anxiety symptoms</sym> (persistent worry, discrete panic spells). These symptoms have persisted for most of the past seven days, interfere with functioning, and meet <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Periparton Onset</med> (onset during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum). Because EPDS is a screening tool and you score in the high-risk range, urgent evaluation is advised. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to review results and discuss treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med>, <med>interpersonal therapy</med>, and/or antidepressant medication compatible with breastfeeding
3. Plan daily 15-minute self-care windows (shower, short walk, brief call with a friend) while a support person cares for the baby
4. Use sleep-hygiene strategies: keep room cool/dark, limit screen time before bed, accept help for night feeds where safe
5. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to track changes after support measures begin
6. Share emergency contacts with your partner: local 24-h crisis line, hospital, and instructions to call 911 if you ever feel unsafe with your thoughts
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant ≤ 6 mo, per history)  
Date: [today]  
Clinician: [name]  

Symptoms endorsed (EPDS-relevant items):
- Anhedonia, diminished pleasure (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt (Q3)  
- Generalized anxiety, nocturnal racing thoughts (Q4)  
- Discrete panic spells (Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed, difficulty coping (Q6)  
- Initial insomnia, hyper-arousal (Q7)  
- Sad mood, tearfulness (Q8, Q9)  

Frequency/severity: Symptoms present “several times per week,” not daily, but interfere with sleep and parenting confidence; no impairment of reality testing or self-harm ideation (Q10 denied).

Pattern: Mixed mood/anxiety presentation; worse evenings; partial functional impact (household tasks, sleep, emotional availability to infant).

Risk factors:  
- Primiparity, sleep deprivation, high self-expectations  
- Absence of suicidal ideation or self-harm intent (safety risk: none reported)

Screening impression:  
Elevated scores consistent with at least mild postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety; recommends full EPDS scoring, clinical interview, and possible referral for evidence-based treatment (CBT, IPT, medication consult). Continue routine monitoring; educate on emergency contacts if worsening mood or safety concerns arise.
